The first Studio Ghibli film to win the Japan Academy Film Prize for Picture of the Year was **“Princess Mononoke” (1997)**.  The film’s critical acclaim was matched by a strong domestic box‑office performance—grossing over ¥5 billion (about US$40 million) in Japan—which helped cement Ghibli’s reputation as a major player in the Japanese film industry.

Its commercial success had a ripple effect internationally.  The high domestic earnings demonstrated that Ghibli’s storytelling and animation could resonate with a wide audience, encouraging distributors abroad to acquire the rights to the film.  “Princess Mononoke” was released in the United States in 1999, where it performed well on the home‑video market and later on television, helping to build a cult following among Western audiences.  The film’s popularity also paved the way for the studio’s subsequent releases—such as *My Neighbor Totoro* and *Spirited Away*—to secure wider theatrical releases overseas, ultimately establishing Studio Ghibli as a globally recognized brand in animation.
